key_points.verbatim: Given that a large number of state-of-the-art models on Natural Language Processing (NLP) tasks are powered by these language generation models, it is of critical importance to properly discover and quantify any existing biases in these models and prevent them from propagating as unfair outcomes and negative experiences to the end users of the downstream applications.

key_points.verbatim: Recently, there has been growing evidence on how machine learning models without proper fairness checks risk reinforcing undesirable stereotypes, subjecting users to disparate treatment and enforcing de facto segregation.

key_points.point: The authors introduce the BOLD dataset to facilitate large-scale, systematic bias benchmarking, which is a core skeptic strategy for holding AI developers accountable. By standardizing metrics for toxicity, sentiment, and gender polarity, they enable the objective measurement of discriminatory impacts. This approach moves beyond anecdotal evidence of bias toward a rigorous, data-driven framework for identifying algorithmic harm.
key_points.verbatim: To systematically study and benchmark social biases in open-ended language generation, we introduce the Bias in Open-Ended Language Generation Dataset (BOLD), a large-scale dataset that consists of 23,679 English text generation prompts for bias benchmarking across five domains: profession, gender, race, religion, and political ideology.

key_points.point: The document provides empirical evidence that language models (LMs) consistently exhibit biases against specific groups, including African Americans and religious groups like Islam. It documents that these models generate more negative sentiment and toxicity toward these groups compared to others. This confirms the skeptic belief that AI models are not neutral but reflect and amplify existing societal prejudices.
key_points.verbatim: For instance, these models more frequently generate texts with negative sentiments and toxicity towards the African American group and more frequently generate text containing male words when a profession context is provided.

key_points.point: The authors observe that models trained on social media data (like CTRL-THT and CTRL-OPN) exhibit higher levels of bias and toxicity than those trained on Wikipedia. This supports the skeptic view that the training data directly dictates the discriminatory output of the model. It highlights the danger of using uncurated, biased human-generated data to train AI systems.
